title: Your MCP Server is Bad (and you should feel bad) - Jeremiah Lowin, Prefect

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is MCP server design, tool calling, and protocol-level best practices for integrating external systems with agents. MCP and FastMCP are developer-facing tools and platforms that other builders use to create agent integrations. The talk covers designing MCP servers, integrating external APIs, and operating them in production with attention to token budgets and performance. Requires familiarity with MCP, REST APIs, and basic agent concepts but is framed as practical guidance rather than advanced research. The content is a conference-style talk by Jeremiah Lowin at the AI Engineer channel. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the talk.

MCP and FastMCP are developer-facing tools and platforms that other builders use to create agent integrations. The talk covers designing MCP servers, integrating external APIs, and operating them in production with attention to token budgets and performance. Requires familiarity with MCP, REST APIs, and basic agent concepts but is framed as practical guidance rather than advanced research. The content is a conference-style talk by Jeremiah Lowin at the AI Engineer channel. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the talk.

summary: Jeremiah Lowin, CEO of Prefect Technologies and creator of FastMCP, presents a talk aimed at improving MCP server quality. He establishes his credentials in data orchestration (Prefect, Apache Airflow) and AI (Marvin agent framework). FastMCP, introduced nearly a year ago, has become the de facto standard for building MCP servers with 1.5 million downloads in a single day. The talk's core thesis is that many MCP servers are bad because they are glorified REST wrappers, treating AIs as if they can use APIs the same way humans do. Lowin rejects the argument that if a human can use an API, an AI can too, noting humans rarely use APIs directly—they use products built on them. Agents deserve their own interfaces optimized for their capabilities. He identifies three dimensions differentiating humans and AIs: discovery (cheap for humans, expensive for AIs), iteration (fast for humans, slow for AIs), and context (rich human memory vs. limited LLM context windows). The most important concept for MCP developers is curation—distilling vast information into small, effective surface areas. Lowin walks through actionable best practices including outcomes over operations (tools should represent complete agent stories, not atomic REST operations), flattening arguments to top-level primitives with literals/enums for constrained choices, and naming tools for agents rather than developers. He covers documentation in depth, noting that undocumented servers cause agents to guess and pollute their history with failed attempts. He introduces the concept that examples are contracts—agents mimic implicit patterns in examples beyond just correctness. He discusses errors as prompts, where error messages become the agent's next input. He covers the MCP read-only annotation hint that clients like ChatGPT use for permission decisions. He emphasizes respecting the token budget, sharing a story about a customer with 800 endpoints where even minimal documentation per tool would lobotomize the agent on handshake. He discusses progressive disclosure techniques, noting Claude Desktop caches tools in SQLite ignoring spec-compliant notifications, and that Prefect's commercial products support per-tool masking. Lowin identifies 50 tools per agent as the threshold where performance degrades. He references Kelly KFL's blog posts about curating a Fiverr MCP server from 188 tools down to five. He strongly advises against converting REST APIs directly into MCP servers for production, though he acknowledges autoconversion as a useful bootstrapping technique. In Q&A, Lowin addresses SEP 1686 (asynchronous background tasks for MCP), noting it is fully opt-in and does not change design rules. He discusses elicitation—structured mid-execution requests for client input—wishing it had better client support so tightly coupled arguments could be moved into elicitation prompts. He advises that MCP servers are unnecessary if you fully control the client and write your own agentic loop, but may provide better observability for tool call failures as the ecosystem matures. He discusses code mode (asking LLMs to write code calling MCP tools in sequence) as an interesting sidestep with sandboxing tradeoffs, noting a FastMCP extension and planned experiments flag. His closing message: MCP servers are user interfaces for agents, not mere tools.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Many MCP servers are bad because they are glorified REST wrappers designed for SDKs, not agents—agents deserve their own interfaces optimized for their capabilities
Three key dimensions differentiate humans and AIs: discovery, iteration, and context—AIs find discovery and iteration expensive and have limited context windows
The most important word for MCP developers is curate—distilling information into small, effective surface areas; 50 tools per agent is the performance degradation threshold
Design for outcomes not operations: each tool should represent a complete agent story, not atomic REST API calls; don't ask agents to be orchestrators
Examples are contracts—agents replicate implicit patterns in examples beyond correctness; errors are prompts that become the agent's next input
Respect the token budget—the handshake downloads all tool descriptions at once; this is the only rule where noncompliance makes a server unusable
Stop converting REST APIs into MCP servers for production—it violates every heuristic discussed; use autoconversion only for bootstrapping, then curate
MCP servers are user interfaces for agents, not mere tools—treat them with the same design care as any user interface

SEP 1686 adds asynchronous background tasks to MCP but is fully opt-in and does not change any design rules; elicitation is promising for tightly coupled arguments and confirmations but lacks sufficient client support
All design principles discussed apply equally to Python tools in agent frameworks, not just MCP servers; MCP servers may offer better observability for tool call failures as the ecosystem matures

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Lowin introduces himself as founder of Prefect Technologies, with history in Apache Airflow, the Marvin agent framework, and FastMCP. He establishes the talk's interactive, off-script format and gauges audience familiarity with MCP.

sections.title: FastMCP Growth and Positioning
sections.summary: FastMCP has become the de facto standard for building MCP servers with 1.5 million daily downloads. It will be positioned as the high-level interface to the MCP ecosystem while the SDK focuses on low-level primitives.

sections.title: Agentic Product Design Motivation
sections.summary: Lowin introduces the core concept of agentic product design, arguing that MCP servers are interfaces for agents and should be designed for agent strengths and weaknesses, just as human products are designed for humans.

sections.title: Three Dimensions: Discovery, Iteration, Context
sections.summary: Lowin details three key differences between humans and AIs: discovery (cheap for humans, expensive for AIs), iteration (fast for humans, slow for AIs), and context (rich human memory vs. limited LLM context windows). He emphasizes the word curate as most important for MCP developers.

sections.title: MCP Overview and Bad Servers Discussion
sections.summary: Lowin briefly covers what MCP is, demonstrates a simple FastMCP server, and opens discussion about why so many bad MCP servers exist. An audience member confirms many are AI wrappers that stringify API content.

sections.title: MCP Best Practices and Outcomes Over Operations
sections.summary: Lowin argues even non-wrapper MCP servers are often bad products due to lack of thought. He praises Block's playbook and GitHub's guidelines as best practice resources. He introduces the first major principle: outcomes over operations—tools should represent complete agent stories, not atomic REST operations. He warns against using agents as orchestrators when algorithms are known. He advises naming tools for agents, not developers.

sections.title: Flattening Arguments and Tool Naming
sections.summary: Lowin presents the second principle: flatten arguments. He warns against complex configuration dictionaries and structured objects, noting Claude Desktop sends object arguments as strings. He recommends top-level primitives, literals, and enums for constrained choices. He also covers naming arguments for the agent.

sections.title: Documentation and Instructions
sections.summary: Lowin discusses the importance of documenting MCP servers and tools. Without instructions, agents will guess and pollute their history with failed attempts. He notes examples in documentation are a double-edged sword and begins discussing this topic.

sections.title: Examples as Contracts and Errors as Prompts
sections.summary: Lowin explains that examples are contracts—agents replicate implicit patterns from examples beyond correctness. He then introduces errors as prompts: error messages become the agent's next input, creating opportunities for progressive disclosure of recovery instructions. He also covers the MCP read-only annotation hint.

sections.title: Token Budget and Progressive Disclosure
sections.summary: Lowin emphasizes respecting the token budget, sharing a story about a customer with 800 endpoints where even minimal per-tool documentation would consume the entire 200,000-token context window on handshake. He discusses progressive disclosure techniques, noting Claude Desktop caches tools in SQLite on first contact, ignoring spec-compliant notifications.

sections.title: Tool Count Thresholds and REST-to-MCP Warning
sections.summary: Lowin discusses 50 tools per agent as the performance degradation threshold. He references Kelly KFL's blog posts about curating a Fiverr server from 188 tools down to five. He strongly warns against converting REST APIs to MCP servers for production, acknowledging autoconversion is popular but should only be used for bootstrapping.

sections.title: Five Principles Recap and Closing Message
sections.summary: Lowin recaps five major principles: outcomes not operations, flatten arguments, instructions as context, respect the token budget, and curate ruthlessly. His closing message: you are building a user interface for an agent, not a tool—treat it accordingly.

sections.title: Q&A: Client Control and Documentation Strategy
sections.summary: In Q&A, Lowin defines tightly coupled arguments and addresses whether to document tools in the server or the agent. If you control the client you can document workflows as Claude skills or files; if you don't, you must document in tool docstrings. He notes the server-level instructions field exists but is not respected by every client.

sections.title: Q&A: Server Instructions, SEP 1686, Elicitation, and Code Mode
sections.summary: Lowin continues Q&A, noting the server instructions blob is another opportunity to document high-level server purpose on handshake but should not be a novel. He discusses SEP 1686, which adds asynchronous background tasks to MCP—fully opt-in, it does not change any design rules. He covers elicitation, a structured mid-execution request for client input, wishing it had better client support so tightly coupled arguments could be moved into elicitation prompts. He advises that MCP servers are unnecessary if you fully control the client and write your own agentic loop, but may provide better observability for tool call failures as the ecosystem matures. He notes all design principles apply equally to Python tools in agent frameworks. He discusses code mode (LLM writes code calling MCP tools in sequence) as an interesting sidestep with sandboxing tradeoffs, mentioning a FastMCP extension and planned experiments flag in the CLI. He thanks the audience and concludes.

limitations: Current MCP client implementations are not amazing and some are non-compliant with the MCP spec
Claude Desktop sends structured object arguments as strings, requiring FastMCP to add deserialization workarounds
Claude Desktop hashes all tools on first contact and caches them in SQLite, ignoring spec-compliant progressive disclosure techniques like notifications
Very few LLMs know that literal/enum syntax is supported, typically defaulting to string parameters
Agent iteration is slow and sends entire history of previous calls over the wire
Examples in documentation are a double-edged sword—agents replicate implicit patterns like array sizes from examples
Error messages that are too aggressive or scary may cause the agent to avoid the tool permanently
The handshake downloads all tool descriptions at once, not progressively disclosed, creating token budget pressure
Progressive disclosure via meta-tools creates complexity where tools are needed to learn about tools
800-endpoint customer could not fit all desired information in the context window and ultimately didn't need to
Server-level instructions field exists but is not respected by every client
REST-to-MCP autoconversion is one of FastMCP's most popular features, making it hard to remove despite being problematic for production
For external-facing servers where you don't control the client, there is no good solution for token budget optimization
Tightly coupled arguments where one argument's input determines valid inputs for another confuse agents
Elicitation lacks sufficient client support because handling it is complicated for automated, backgrounded, or non-user-facing clients
Code mode introduces sandboxing and code execution problems that offset its benefits

Ideal target is 5-15 tools per server
